metadata.title: Rates, Speed and Best Buys
metadata.vcaa_description: Recognise and use rates to solve problems involving the comparison of 2 related quantities of different units of measure.
metadata.target_mastery: Calculate and convert unit rates, compare Australian supermarket products using unit pricing ($/100 g or $/L), and solve distance-speed-time and fuel consumption problems.
prerequisites: Dividing decimals and converting metric units

key_vocabulary.definition: A comparison of two related quantities measured in different units, written with 'per' or a slash `/` (e.g., $\text{km/h}$, $\text{\$/kg}$, $\text{L/min}$).
A simplified rate in which the second quantity is $1\text{ unit}$ (e.g., $95\text{ km}$ per $1\text{ hour}$).
Comparing the cost of different package sizes by calculating the price per standard unit (such as per $100\text{ g}$, per $\text{kg}$, or per $\text{L}$).

theory.title: Simplifying Rates and Supermarket Unit Pricing (Best Buys)
theory.explanation: Unlike ratios, rates always retain their units because they compare two different types of measurement (such as dollars and grams). To simplify a rate $A\text{ units}_1 \text{ per } B\text{ units}_2$, divide $A$ by $B$ to get the amount per $1\text{ unit}_2$. Australian supermarkets display unit prices (typically per $100\text{ g}$ or per $1\text{ L}$) so shoppers can identify the 'best buy' (lowest unit cost).
theory.callout_title: Order of Division matches the Slash
theory.callout_rule: The word 'per' (or `/`) means DIVIDE! Dollars per kilogram ($\text{\$/kg}$) means $\text{Dollars} \div \text{Kilograms}$.

theory.title: Average Speed, Distance, and Time
theory.explanation: Average speed is the rate of distance travelled per unit of time. The three quantities Distance ($D$), Average Speed ($S$), and Time ($T$) are linked by three equivalent formulas.
theory.callout_rule: Since $1\text{ km} = 1000\text{ m}$ and $1\text{ h} = 3600\text{ s}$, $1\text{ m/s} = \frac{3600}{1000}\text{ km/h} = 3.6\text{ km/h}$. Multiply $\text{m/s}$ by $3.6$ to get $\text{km/h}$; divide $\text{km/h}$ by $3.6$ to get $\text{m/s}$.

theory.title: Fuel Consumption Rate ($\text{L/100 km}$)
theory.explanation: In Australia, motor vehicle fuel efficiency is rated in litres of fuel consumed per $100\text{ km}$ driven ($\text{L/100 km}$).
theory.callout_rule: If a car uses $7.5\text{ L/100 km}$, then for a $400\text{ km}$ trip ($4$ lots of $100\text{ km}$), it uses $4 \times 7.5 = 30\text{ L}$ of fuel.

worked_examples.title: Supermarket Best Buy Comparison
worked_examples.problem: At a supermarket in Box Hill, Australian rolled oats are sold in two sizes: a $750\text{ g}$ box for $\$4.50$, or a $1.2\text{ kg}$ bag for $\$6.60$. Calculate the cost per $100\text{ g}$ for each option and state which is the better buy.

steps.thinking: For the $750\text{ g}$ box ($7.5$ lots of $100\text{ g}$), divide $\$4.50$ by $7.5$.
Convert $1.2\text{ kg}$ to $1200\text{ g}$ ($12$ lots of $100\text{ g}$) and divide $\$6.60$ by $12$.
Compare the unit prices: $\$0.55 < \$0.60$, so the $1.2\text{ kg}$ bag is cheaper per $100\text{ g}$.
steps.working: $$\$0.55/100\text{ g} < \$0.60/100\text{ g} \implies 1.2\text{ kg bag is the best buy}$$

worked_examples.final_answer: Option A: $\$0.60/100\text{ g}$; Option B: $\$0.55/100\text{ g}$. The $1.2\text{ kg}$ bag is the better buy.

now_you_try.problem: Olive oil is sold in a $500\text{ mL}$ bottle for $\$7.50$ or a $750\text{ mL}$ bottle for $\$10.50$. Find the cost per $100\text{ mL}$ for each and identify the best buy.
now_you_try.answer: The $750\text{ mL}$ bottle ($\$1.40/100\text{ mL}$) is the better buy.

worked_examples.title: Speed, Distance, Time and $\text{m/s} \leftrightarrow \text{km/h}$ Conversion
worked_examples.problem: (a) Convert a sprinter's speed of $10\text{ m/s}$ into $\text{km/h}$. (b) A V/Line train travels $180\text{ km}$ from Melbourne to Shepparton in $2\text{ hours } 15\text{ minutes}$. Find its average speed in $\text{km/h}$.

steps.thinking: Convert $2\text{ hours } 15\text{ minutes}$ to hours: $15\text{ minutes} = \frac{15}{60} = 0.25\text{ hours}$, so $T = 2.25\text{ hours}$. Divide $D = 180\text{ km}$ by $T = 2.25\text{ h}$.

now_you_try.problem: (a) Convert $90\text{ km/h}$ into $\text{m/s}$. (b) How far does a car travelling at an average speed of $96\text{ km/h}$ travel in $1\text{ hour } 45\text{ minutes}$?
now_you_try.hint: Divide $90$ by $3.6$ for (a), and write $1\text{ h } 45\text{ min} = 1.75\text{ h}$ for (b).

worked_examples.title: Australian Highway Fuel Consumption Modelling
worked_examples.problem: A family drives $650\text{ km}$ along the Hume Highway from Melbourne to Canberra. Their car has an average fuel consumption of $6.8\text{ L/100 km}$, and unleaded petrol costs $\$2.00\text{ per litre}$. Find (a) the total volume of fuel used and (b) the total fuel cost for the trip.

steps.thinking: Express $650\text{ km}$ as $6.5$ lots of $100\text{ km}$ and multiply by $6.8\text{ L/100 km}$.
Multiply the $44.2\text{ L}$ of fuel by $\$2.00\text{/L}$.

now_you_try.problem: A ute uses $49.5\text{ L}$ of diesel to travel $550\text{ km}$ across outback Victoria. Calculate its fuel consumption rate in $\text{L/100 km}$.
now_you_try.hint: Divide $49.5\text{ L}$ by $5.5$ (the number of hundreds of kilometres).

common_misconceptions.title: Writing Hours and Minutes Directly as a Base-10 Decimal
common_misconceptions.misconception: Writing $2\text{ hours } 30\text{ minutes}$ as $2.3\text{ hours}$, or $1\text{ hour } 15\text{ minutes}$ as $1.15\text{ hours}$, when calculating $D = S \times T$.
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: There are $60\text{ minutes}$ in $1\text{ hour}$, not $100$. Always divide the minutes by $60$: $30\text{ min} = \frac{30}{60} = 0.5\text{ h}$ (so $2.5\text{ h}$), and $15\text{ min} = \frac{15}{60} = 0.25\text{ h}$ (so $1.25\text{ h}$).
common_misconceptions.counter_example: At $100\text{ km/h}$ for $2\text{ hours } 30\text{ minutes}$, you travel $250\text{ km}$ ($100 \times 2.5$), not $230\text{ km}$.

common_misconceptions.title: Averaging Two Speeds Instead of Dividing Total Distance by Total Time
common_misconceptions.misconception: If a cyclist rides $30\text{ km}$ uphill at $15\text{ km/h}$ and $30\text{ km}$ back downhill at $30\text{ km/h}$, assuming the average speed for the whole trip is $\frac{15 + 30}{2} = 22.5\text{ km/h}$.
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: Because the cyclist spends more time travelling at the slower uphill speed ($2\text{ h}$ uphill vs $1\text{ h}$ downhill), average speed is always $\frac{\text{Total Distance}}{\text{Total Time}} = \frac{60\text{ km}}{3\text{ h}} = 20\text{ km/h}$.
common_misconceptions.counter_example: The total trip of $60\text{ km}$ took $3\text{ hours}$ in total, which is exactly $20\text{ km}$ per hour.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Express $\$136$ earned in $8\text{ hours}$ as a unit rate in $\text{\$/h}$.
step_by_step_solution: Write the rate as a fraction: $\frac{\$136}{8\text{ hours}}$.
Divide the dollars earned by the number of hours: $136 \div 8 = \$17\text{/h}$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Convert $108\text{ km/h}$ into $\text{m/s}$.
step_by_step_solution: Recall that converting from $\text{km/h}$ to $\text{m/s}$ requires dividing by $3.6$.
Evaluate $108 \div 3.6 = 30\text{ m/s}$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Convert $15\text{ m/s}$ into $\text{km/h}$.
step_by_step_solution: Recall that converting from $\text{m/s}$ to $\text{km/h}$ requires multiplying by $3.6$.
Evaluate $15 \times 3.6 = 54\text{ km/h}$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: A water pump fills a $3600\text{ L}$ rainwater tank in $45\text{ minutes}$. Express this flow rate in (a) $\text{L/min}$ and (b) $\text{L/h}$.
step_by_step_solution: Divide $3600\text{ L}$ by $45\text{ minutes}$: $3600 \div 45 = 80\text{ L/min}$.
Multiply by $60\text{ minutes/hour}$: $80 \times 60 = 4800\text{ L/h}$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: How many minutes does it take a runner moving at a constant speed of $4\text{ m/s}$ to complete a $3.6\text{ km}$ cross-country course?
step_by_step_solution: Convert $3.6\text{ km}$ to metres: $3600\text{ m}$.
Calculate time in seconds: $T = 3600 \div 4 = 900\text{ seconds}$.
Convert seconds to minutes: $900 \div 60 = 15\text{ minutes}$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Australian honey is sold in three jar sizes: $250\text{ g}$ for $\$4.25$, $400\text{ g}$ for $\$6.40$, and $750\text{ g}$ for $\$12.30$. Find the price per $100\text{ g}$ for each jar and state the best buy.
fluency_and_understanding.final_answer: $400\text{ g}$ jar ($\$1.60/100\text{ g}$) is the best buy
step_by_step_solution: The $400\text{ g}$ jar has the lowest unit price ($\$1.60/100\text{ g}$).

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A motorist drives from Melbourne to Warrnambool: the first $180\text{ km}$ takes $2\text{ hours}$, and the remaining $80\text{ km}$ takes $1\text{ hour } 15\text{ minutes}$. Find the motorist's overall average speed for the entire journey in $\text{km/h}$.
step_by_step_solution: Total distance $= 180 + 80 = 260\text{ km}$.
Total time $= 2 + 1.25 = 3.25\text{ hours}$.
Overall average speed $= 260 \div 3.25 = 80\text{ km/h}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: Two taps are used together to fill an $1800\text{ L}$ spa pool. Tap A flows at $18\text{ L/min}$ and Tap B flows at $12\text{ L/min}$. How many minutes will it take to fill the pool when both taps are turned on simultaneously?
step_by_step_solution: Add the two flow rates to find the combined rate: $18 + 12 = 30\text{ L/min}$.
Divide the total volume by the combined rate: $1800 \div 30 = 60\text{ minutes}$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A hybrid SUV uses $5.2\text{ L/100 km}$ while a conventional petrol SUV uses $8.7\text{ L/100 km}$. If a Melbourne driver travels $15\,000\text{ km}$ per year and petrol costs $\$2.00\text{/L}$, how much money in fuel costs does the hybrid SUV save per year?
step_by_step_solution: Fuel saved per $100\text{ km}$: $8.7 - 5.2 = 3.5\text{ L/100 km}$.
Over $15\,000\text{ km}$ ($150$ lots of $100\text{ km}$), fuel saved $= 150 \times 3.5 = 525\text{ L}$.
Dollar savings at $\$2.00\text{/L}$: $525 \times 2.00 = \$1050$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Prove from first principles (using $1\text{ km} = 1000\text{ m}$ and $1\text{ h} = 3600\text{ s}$) why converting from $\text{m/s}$ to $\text{km/h}$ requires multiplying by $3.6$.
step_by_step_solution: An object moving at $v\text{ m/s}$ travels $v\text{ metres}$ in $1\text{ second}$.
In $1\text{ hour}$ ($3600\text{ seconds}$), it travels $3600v\text{ metres}$.
Dividing by $1000$ to convert metres to kilometres gives $\frac{3600v}{1000} = 3.6v\text{ km/h}$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Train A leaves Southern Cross Station at $9\text{:00 am}$ travelling west at $80\text{ km/h}$. Train B leaves the same station at $9\text{:30 am}$ on a parallel track travelling west at $100\text{ km/h}$. At what time does Train B catch up to Train A, and how far from the station are they?
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: $11\text{:30 am}$ at $200\text{ km}$ from the station
step_by_step_solution: By $9\text{:30 am}$ ($0.5\text{ h}$), Train A has a head start of $80 \times 0.5 = 40\text{ km}$.
Train B closes the gap at a relative speed of $100 - 80 = 20\text{ km/h}$.
Time to close the $40\text{ km}$ gap: $40 \div 20 = 2\text{ hours}$ after $9\text{:30 am}$, which is $11\text{:30 am}$.
Distance from station: $2 \times 100 = 200\text{ km}$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Painter A can paint a fence in $6\text{ hours}$ alone, and Painter B can paint the same fence in $4\text{ hours}$ alone. By expressing their work rates in 'fences per hour', find how many hours and minutes it takes them to paint $1$ fence working together.
step_by_step_solution: Painter A's rate is $\frac{1}{6}$ fence/hour and Painter B's rate is $\frac{1}{4}$ fence/hour.
Combined rate $= \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{2 + 3}{12} = \frac{5}{12}$ fences/hour.
Time to paint $1$ fence $= 1 \div \frac{5}{12} = \frac{12}{5} = 2\frac{2}{5}\text{ hours} = 2\text{ hours } 24\text{ minutes}$.
